title: Lecture 8. Semi-structured interview (individual, group, focus groups)
summary:
=== LESSON 8. Semi-structured interview (individual, group, focus groups) ===

A semi-structured interview differs from an unstructured one by having a plan. The researcher is not obliged to strictly adhere to it; the sequence of discussed questions should follow the logic of the interview, but answers must be obtained for all questions. (It is worth noting that a well-prepared guide is unlikely to contradict the natural flow of the interview).

A semi-structured interview is used when it is necessary to obtain certain information from a specific target group on a particular topic. This procedure, unlike an unstructured interview, implies the possibility of not only qualitative but also quantitative processing of results. In an educational organization, this method can be applied to ascertain the opinions of target prevention groups on various issues, for example, students' attitudes towards certain problems, or the readiness of educators to participate in specific preventive measures.

Moreover, it can be expected that both during individual interviews and group work, representatives of the target group will express thoughts and reveal the true causes of certain problems that cannot be obtained by any other means. Even in a clinical interview, a respondent may conceal some thoughts or find it difficult to articulate them. But in conditions of group dynamics, during a lively discussion or when defending the opinion of a certain group, people more often formulate ideas hidden even from themselves.

A semi-structured interview can be used within a study as an auxiliary tool to a population survey – for formulating answer options for closed questions, or to assist in interpreting survey results.

A semi-structured interview is conducted using a special document called a guide, which includes a list of PROGRAMMATIC research questions. It is important to note that this distinguishes such an interview from a questionnaire, where questions are formulated directly for the respondent. In the guide, questions are formulated for the researcher, who must reformulate them into a form suitable for the situation and the logic of the interview.

For example, a guide for interviewing experts in drug policy, whether individual or group, might look as follows.

Factors influencing drug use: a) in the territory as a whole, b) in key risk groups. Potential and actual opportunities to counteract these factors. Problems and difficulties in implementing anti-drug policy in the region. Possible solutions to the listed problems. Desirable changes in the organization of anti-drug policy at the level of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation, district level, and federal level. Proposals for improving the system of accounting and evaluation of preventive anti-drug work. The results of a semi-structured interview are processed using qualitative-quantitative analysis (or content analysis), which is applied when studying sources invariant in structure or content. In the first stage of such analysis, the main semantic blocks on which respondents expressed their opinions are identified. Then, all respondents' statements are grouped into these semantic blocks, with similar statements being formulated into identical phrases. Subsequently, identical phrases are summed up, and their quantity is indicated. Thus, the result is a "weighted average" opinion of the studied group on the questions in the interview guide. In reality, there are many subtleties in the procedure of such analysis, which can be read about in specialized manuals.

The final presentation of semi-structured interview results may look as follows in a tabular form, for which a textual analytical report is subsequently prepared.
